newsitem.title: USA: Alaskans eye petroleum reserve and gas-line plan.
newsitem.headline: Alaskans eye petroleum reserve and gas-line plan.

text.p: New oil development in a vast, federally owned reserve west of Prudhoe Bay and a new pipeline to transport the North Slope's 26 trillion cubic feet of natural gas could fuel the next Alaska petroleum booms, officials said.

The state, Inupiat Eskimos of the North Slope and oil companies are eyeing new oil opportunities in the 23 million-acre National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska (NPRA), a flat federal property that stretches west of Prudhoe Bay to the Chukchi Sea.

The petroleum reserve, established by President Warren Harding in 1923, has been explored in the past, but oil and gas discoveries there were seen as too small to justify commercial development. The most active exploration occurred in the 1940s and 1950s, but some federal leases were sold as recently as the 1980s.
Now many oil experts say modern exploration techniques could help detect commercial quantities of oil in NRPA.

Interest was sharpened by the recent discovery of the a major oil deposit in the Colville River delta on the eastern edge of the reserve. The Alpine field, discovered by Arco, Anadarko and Union Texas Petroleum, holds 250 million to 300 million recoverable barrels.

While the Clinton administration vehemently objects to oil development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) east of Prudhoe Bay, it is considering new oil development in NPRA, either through a leasing programme or a land trade, said Deborah Williams, a special assistant to U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt.

Environmentalists oppose oil drilling in the ANWR coastal plain, a narrow strip bounded by the Brooks Range and the Arctic Ocean, because of possible damage to the caribou, musk oxen and other wildlife there.
Environmentalists appear more ambivalent about oil development in NRPA.

"It's an area that is available for oil and gas leasing," conceded Jack Hession, Alaska representative to the Sierra Club. "The controversy will be over how and where leasing will occur, assuming the Department of Interior goes through with it."
He said certain "special places" that are important to caribou, migratory birds and other wildlife should be protected from oil development, and a new environmental impact study should be done.
The natural gas pipeline project, meanwhile, has some appeal to environmentalists and is supported by the Clinton administration.
Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles said he plans to introduce legislation to create state tax incentives to help lower the pipeline's construction cost, now estimated at $13 billion.
For now, North Slope gas is used primarily as an aid in recovering additional oil from the maturing fields. It is reinjected into the ground to increase reservoir pressure.
The future market for North Slope gas sales is seen as Japan, Korea, Taiwan and possibly other Asian countries.
The governor said Asian markets will be ready for North Slope gas in seven to 10 years -- about the same time that the gas's usefulness in extracting oil will be exhausted.
"Their needs fit in with our availability," he said.
It is possible that Asian customers will pay a premium for gas from Alaska, he said. "They don't want to put all of their eggs in the Mideast basket," he said.
